paras: The lynching of Dave Southall was the killing of a Black man by a large crowd of masked men in Louisiana on the night of Sunday, 13 May 1888, as a deputy sheriff took him through the country after his arrest. Southall had been charged with raising a mob and attempting to kill a man who had challenged his right to vote in Pointe Coupee Parish. A single New Orleans dispatch about the killing ran in at least thirteen papers across the country, under headlines that ranged from 'Lynched in Louisiana' to 'A Case of Poetic Justice'.

According to the dispatch, Southall, described as 'a colored man of Pointe Coupee', was said to live in Iberville Parish. Just after an election, a Mr. Garnet challenged his right to vote in Pointe Coupee, and Southall was then charged with raising a mob and attempting to kill Garnet on Bayou Grosse. The Savannah Morning News version said 'attacking' rather than 'attempting to kill', and its deck stated that 'The Dead Man Had Raised a Mob During Political Excitement'.
When Sheriff Beaukor (spelled Beauker, Becker and Baker in other copies) went to arrest him, Southall fled the parish. He was arrested in Baton Rouge on Saturday, 12 May.

On Sunday night Deputy Sheriff Caldwell was taking Southall through the country in a buggy when a large crowd of masked men surrounded them. The men dragged Southall from the buggy and 'disarmed him', a phrase that most likely refers to the deputy but does not say so. They then took Southall some distance away and shot him dead.
The coverage does not identify any member of the crowd or report an inquest, arrest or prosecution.

Every account found is the same telegraphic dispatch datelined New Orleans, 15 May, though a few copies carried a 16 May date. It appeared first on 15 May in the Alexandria Gazette and the San Antonio Daily Light, then on 16 May in Fort Worth, Memphis, Richmond, Savannah and Springfield, Ohio. Papers in Texas, Kansas, Mississippi, Georgia, Missouri and Indiana reprinted it through 25 May, and the Butler Weekly Times in Missouri cut it to a few lines that dropped Iberville, the bayou and the sheriff.

The text itself was terse and gave the charge against Southall without qualification, and the headlines supplied most of the framing. The Alexandria Gazette headed it 'Negro Lawbreaker Killed' and the San Antonio Daily Light 'Negro Rioter Shot by Masked Men', labels that treated the accusation as settled. The Memphis Appeal went further with 'A Case of Poetic Justice', while the Savannah Morning News called it plainly 'Lynched in Louisiana'. Most other papers used neutral headings such as 'Taken From the Sheriff and Shot' and 'Killed by a Mob'.

Spellings of the names drifted from copy to copy, with Garnet appearing as Garnett, Girnet, Gernet and Geinet, and the bayou as Bayou Grosse, Grosse Tele and 'Cross Teche'. No account from a Louisiana paper, and none from the Black press, appears in the coverage.

Southall, charged with raising a mob and attempting to kill a white man who had challenged his vote, was taken from a deputy by 'a large crowd of masked men' and shot dead without any legal process (A1, A4, A6).
Every report is the same New Orleans wire dispatch of May 15, reprinted with minor variants (A1, A2, A6, A12); no local or independent account was found.

accounts.label: New Orleans wire report
accounts.gist: Southall, charged with raising a mob and attempting to kill Mr. Garnet over a challenged vote, was arrested at Baton Rouge, then taken from Deputy Caldwell's buggy by a large crowd of masked men and shot dead on Sunday night.

framing.detail: The Memphis Appeal headed the wire 'A Case of Poetic Justice', treating the killing as deserved.
The Alexandria Gazette and San Antonio Daily Light labeled Southall 'Negro Lawbreaker' and 'Negro Rioter' in their headlines over the wire text.
The Savannah Morning News headed it 'Lynched in Louisiana' with the deck 'The Dead Man Had Raised a Mob During Political Excitement'.
Other papers used plain headlines such as 'Taken From the Sheriff and Shot' and 'Killed by a Mob'.
